lesson.menu_title: You Have Been There, Have You Not?
lesson.menu_desc: Phase 4 -- keep a conversation going with people you meet on a trip, with question tags and the intonation that goes with them -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 36 -- You Have Been There, Have You Not? -- Question Tags
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 36 -- You Have Been There, Have You Not?
lesson.grammar_point: question tags (same auxiliary and opposite polarity, do/does/did when there is no auxiliary, I am... aren't I, let's... shall we, imperatives with will you, negative words like never and nobody, and falling vs rising intonation)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you told the story of a trip through what was done. Today you talk to the people on that trip. When you meet somebody on a train, a direct question like have you been to Osaka is correct, but it sounds like a form. A question tag sounds like a conversation. You say what you think is true, and you add a tiny question. You've been to Osaka, haven't you? The rule is simple. Copy the auxiliary from the sentence, and turn it around. A positive sentence gets a negative tag, and a negative sentence gets a positive one. You didn't take the fast train, did you? If there is no auxiliary, use do, does or did. She likes sushi, doesn't she? There are a few special ones. I'm late becomes aren't I. Let's go becomes shall we. And an instruction becomes will you. Now the traps. In Portuguese, one little word works for everything, and many Brazilians use isn't it for every sentence. It only works after it is. Second, never and nobody are already negative, so the tag is positive. Nobody told you, did they? And third, listen to your voice. If it goes down, you are sure. If it goes up, it is a real question. Before class, write ten sentences about the trip, each with a tag.

Okay, everybody, welcome to Kamo River Hostel. You all found us without any problems, didn't you? Good. I'm Kenji, and this kitchen is the heart of the house, so you'll spend a lot of time here, won't you? Let me explain a few things. Breakfast isn't included, but there's plenty of rice and tea, and nobody will charge you for that, will they? You've all taken your shoes off, haven't you? Great. Now, most of you have never been to Kyoto before, have you? Then here is my one piece of advice. Talk to each other. Half of the best stories I hear started in this kitchen, with somebody saying something like, you're from Brazil, aren't you? Tonight a few of us are going to the night market by the river. You can tag along if you want. It's not far, and it's free. Let's meet here at seven, shall we? Oh, and one last thing. Keep your voices down after eleven, will you? The walls are thin. Enjoy your stay.

extra_audio.text: Excuse me, this train goes to Osaka, doesn't it? It does. You're not from here, are you? No, I'm from Brazil. You've been to Osaka before, haven't you? Many times. My cousin lives there. I could show you around the market, if you like. That would be great. Let's meet at the station at ten, shall we?

reading.rtitle: The Question That Keeps Conversations Going
paras: Ask any traveler about the best part of a trip, and a surprising number of them will not mention a place. They will mention a person: somebody they bumped into on a train, a chatty cook at a ramen counter, a fellow traveler who showed them around a city for an afternoon. Meeting people is the part of travel that nobody can book in advance.

The problem is the first minute. Most of us are bad at small talk with strangers, and a direct question can make things awkward. "Where are you from?" sounds like a form at the border. Our writer noticed that the travelers who hit it off with people fastest all did the same small thing. They said what they thought, and they added a tiny question at the end.

"You're from Brazil, aren't you?" is not really a question. It is an invitation. The speaker already thinks the answer is yes, so the other person does not have to think. They just agree, and they usually say something more. "I am! From Sao Paulo. You've been there, haven't you?" In ten seconds the ice is broken, and each tag keeps the ball rolling a little longer.

There is one secret that grammar books do not always explain. The voice matters as much as the words. When the voice goes down at the end, you are checking something you are sure about. When it goes up, it becomes a real question. Get that right, and people open up. And if you are still not sure, remember that nobody expects a tourist to be perfect, do they?
reading.source: The Corridor -- student paper, travel page
